concepts.name: Tab sequence and internal widget focus

questions.prompt: An icon-only delete button has no text alternative. Which change addresses its accessible name?

choices.text: Provide a description while leaving the button without any identifying accessible name.
Rely on the SVG filename to supply the parent button name automatically in every case.
Mark the button presentation-only so its icon becomes the only interactive control.
Provide a concise accessible name such as `Delete item`.

questions.explanation: An icon-only button needs an identifying accessible name. A description is supplemental, filenames are not reliable automatic names, and hiding button semantics removes useful control information.

sources.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions
sources.claim: Controls need accessible names; native labels and visible text are preferred and descriptions provide additional context rather than replacing names.

questions.prompt: A clickable div gets `role=button` but has no keyboard handling. What did the role itself add?

choices.text: Native Enter and Space activation, because role alone implements button behavior.
An automatic focusable tab stop, because every ARIA role supplies browser focus behavior.
Button semantics, while keyboard behavior still needs implementation.
Native form submission, because role changes the div into a button element.

questions.explanation: ARIA communicates semantics; it does not turn a div into a native button or implement its keyboard interaction.

sources.title: Developing a Keyboard Interface
sources.claim: ARIA does not implement keyboard behavior; composite widgets manage internal focus while Tab moves between components, and focus remains visible.

questions.prompt: A menu contains many items. Which keyboard design follows the usual composite convention?

choices.text: Tab visits every internal item while arrows are reserved for scrolling the page.
Tab enters or leaves the component; arrow keys navigate within it.
Arrow keys move between separate components while Tab moves only inside this menu.
The menu traps Tab permanently so focus cannot reach the next page component.

questions.explanation: Composite widgets generally use Tab between components and arrows inside. Trapping Tab is not the general convention.

sources.title: Developing a Keyboard Interface
sources.claim: ARIA does not implement keyboard behavior; composite widgets manage internal focus while Tab moves between components, and focus remains visible.

questions.prompt: A selected tab keeps a colored background after focus moves elsewhere. What must the UI still communicate?

choices.text: The current keyboard focus separately from the selected state.
Only the selected state, because selection always identifies the currently focused item.
Only hover styling, because pointer position and keyboard focus always coincide.
No visual indicator, because a supplied ARIA selected state replaces focus visibility.

questions.explanation: Focus and selection can differ. Keyboard users need a discernible focus indicator even when selected styling persists.

sources.claim: ARIA does not implement keyboard behavior; composite widgets manage internal focus while Tab moves between components, and focus remains visible.

questions.prompt: A search field needs both a short name and instructions about accepted syntax. What is the appropriate relationship?

choices.text: Use the long instructions as a description and omit the identifying name entirely.
Use a placeholder as the only name and rely on it remaining visible after typing.
Use only a title tooltip and omit the visible field label and persistent instructions.
Use a name for identification and a description for additional instructions.

questions.explanation: The accessible name identifies the control; the description adds usage instructions. A description does not replace a name, and visible labels avoid dependence on transient placeholders or tooltips.

sources.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions

questions.prompt: A team needs a simple action button without a custom interaction pattern. Which starting point reduces keyboard implementation work?

choices.text: Use a div with role=button and assume that the role supplies keyboard activation.
Use a span with a click listener and assume it receives a native focus stop.
Use a native button with an appropriate text name.
Use an image with a mouse handler and assume its alt text supplies button behavior.

questions.explanation: Native HTML form controls supply keyboard support. ARIA widgets require authors to implement their interaction.

questions.prompt: A review checks names and descriptions. Which choices are sound? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Give an icon button a useful accessible name.
Prefer visible labels when they can name a control.
Every placeholder provides a persistent visible label after the user types.
Use an accessible description instead of any identifying accessible name.
Assume every unlabeled SVG gives its parent a useful name.

questions.explanation: a: The control must be identifiable without interpreting the icon. b: Visible text helps multiple users and reduces mismatches. c: Placeholders disappear as users enter text and are not persistent visible labels. d: A description supplements a name and does not replace it. e: An icon needs deliberate naming; SVG existence is insufficient.

sources.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions
sources.claim: Controls need accessible names; native labels and visible text are preferred and descriptions provide additional context rather than replacing names.

questions.prompt: A custom div has an ARIA role. Which implementation responsibilities remain? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Manage focus where the widget pattern requires it.
Assume ARIA changes the underlying DOM element type.
Prefer native controls for simple supported interactions.
Adding role=button alone supplies Enter and Space activation.
Implement the appropriate keyboard interaction.

questions.explanation: a: Authors must implement the interaction pattern. b: A role supplies semantics without replacing the element. c: Their browser-provided behavior reduces custom work. d: ARIA supplies semantics but the author implements keyboard behavior. e: ARIA does not supply keyboard behavior.

questions.prompt: A composite widget has internal focusable items. Which conventions hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Every internal item must always be a separate Tab stop.
Every composite item must use the same Tab-only navigation as a plain link.
Every composite should trap Tab indefinitely.
Tab usually moves between UI components.
Arrow keys commonly navigate within a composite.

questions.explanation: a: A composite commonly has one entry in the tab sequence. b: Composite patterns commonly use managed internal focus and arrow keys. c: Users must be able to move to the next component. d: This is the primary page navigation convention. e: Patterns provide the expected internal movement.

questions.prompt: An interface highlights selected items. Which focus decisions hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Check custom indicators in high-contrast modes.
Selected styling alone identifies keyboard focus after focus moves elsewhere.
Keep the location of keyboard focus discernible.
Distinguish selection styling from focus styling.
Remove every focus indicator because selection exists.

questions.explanation: a: Custom visual styles may disappear or become unclear. b: Selection may persist on an item that no longer has focus. c: Users need to know where keyboard actions will apply. d: The selected item may not currently have focus. e: Selection does not replace a focus indication.
